# Preface {.unnumbered}

**PhyloTrace** is a platform for bacterial pathogen monitoring on a genomic
level. It turns whole-genome assemblies into allele profiles by core-genome
multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST), screens them for antimicrobial-resistance
determinants, and enables exploration of the relationships between isolates
through interactive minimum spanning trees, phylogenetic trees, epidemic
curves, maps and heatmaps — all from a local, portable database under your
full control.

This manual is the **user's reference** for that system. It explains what each
part of the app does, the science behind it, and how to use it in practice.

## Who this manual is for

Epidemiologists, microbiologists and laboratory staff who want to run genomic
surveillance work in PhyloTrace. It assumes **no programming background**: there
is no R to read, no code to write, and no command line to use.

::: {.callout-note title="Looking for the code?"}
Everything about how PhyloTrace is *built* — its module structure, database
schema, the exact functions behind each pipeline, and the conventions for
extending it — lives in the separate **technical manual** under
`docs/technical/`. This book deliberately leaves that material out so it can stay
about using the app.
:::

## How to read it {#sec-conventions}

The manual uses a small, consistent set of conventions so you can find your way
through it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept"}
Boxes like this explain an idea — what a minimum spanning tree is, why allelic
distance measures relatedness — at an abstract level and in plain language.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Good to know"}
Boxes like this flag something about the app's behaviour that is easy to
misread: what a control actually does, when a result is a genotype rather than a
phenotype, or when a number should not be over-interpreted.
:::

### Finding a control in the app {#sec-conventions-ui}

Everything you can click is named in the manual exactly as it is labelled on
screen, in **bold**. Where a control is buried more than one level deep, the
whole route is written out with `>` between the steps, from the navigation tab
inwards:

> **Visualization > Options > Clustering > Threshold (allelic distance)**

reads as: the Visualization tab, the **Options** tab of the plot's own control
panel, the **Clustering** section inside it, and the numeric field labelled
*Threshold (allelic distance)*. Screenshots of each panel accompany the text, so
a route can always be checked against the picture.

Cross-references such as @sec-typing are clickable, as are figure references (for
example @fig-preface-workflow below) and citations such as the original MLST
description [@maiden1998mlst]. The full bibliography is on the
[References](references.qmd) page, and @sec-glossary defines every term the
manual uses.

::: {.callout-important title="Every statement about the data has a control behind it"}
Wherever the manual says that PhyloTrace does something to your data — merges
identical isolates, picks a cluster threshold, bins dates into weeks, drops
undated cases — it also names the control that governs it, because almost none
of those behaviours is fixed. Defaults are chosen to be defensible, not to be
permanent, and a figure you publish should be described by the settings you
actually used rather than by the ones the app opened with.
:::

## The workflow at a glance

Although PhyloTrace is fully interactive, the work it supports can be broken
down into a linear workflow. Each stage is a chapter of this manual.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-preface-workflow
%%| fig-cap: "The PhyloTrace workflow. Each stage maps to a chapter in this manual. Dashed edges show the database's portability (export/import between labs); the solid loop back from the Analysis Dashboard shows that saved plots persist inside the same database file."
flowchart LR
  A["Whole-genome<br/>assemblies (FASTA)"] --> B["Scheme<br/>management"]
  B --> C1["cgMLST typing<br/>(core genome)"]
  B --> C2["Classical MLST<br/>(7-gene ST)"]
  B --> E["AMR<br/>screening"]
  C1 --> D[("Local database<br/>(one portable file)")]
  C2 --> D
  E --> D
  D -. "export" .-> P[("Peer lab's<br/>database")]
  P -. "import" .-> D
  D --> F["Browse &amp;<br/>curate"]
  D --> G["Visualize<br/>(MST · Tree · Epi · Map · Heatmap)"]
  G --> H["Analysis Dashboard<br/>(saved plots)"]
  H --> D
```

## Structure of this manual {#sec-roadmap}

**Part I · Orientation** — what PhyloTrace is (@sec-intro) and the scientific
concepts behind it (@sec-concepts): assemblies, loci and alleles, the core
genome, allelic profiles and sequence types, allelic distance, minimum spanning
trees, phylogenetic trees, AMR markers, epidemic curves and content hashing.

**Part II · The App & Your Data** — how the application behaves as you work in it
(@sec-app-basics), and what your database file contains and how to look after it
(@sec-data).

**Part III · Components** — the parts of the app you work through, in the order a
new dataset passes through them: scheme management (@sec-schemes), allelic typing
(@sec-typing), AMR screening (@sec-amr), the database browser and custom
variables (@sec-browser), and sharing data with other labs (@sec-interop). Taken
together these form the app's pipelines.

**Part IV · Visualization & Analysis** — the plot workspace (@sec-visualization),
minimum spanning trees (@sec-mst), phylogenetic trees (@sec-trees), epidemic
curves (@sec-epicurve), maps (@sec-map), AMR heatmaps (@sec-amr-heatmap), and the
Analysis Dashboard where finished work is saved (@sec-dashboard).

**Appendices** — the external tools and data sources PhyloTrace uses
(@sec-appendix-tools), a glossary (@sec-glossary), and the
[References](references.qmd).

*PhyloTrace is intended for research and academic purposes only.*
